title: Daylighting in Schools An Investigation into the Relationship Between Daylighting and Human Performance Condensed Report
research_question: To investigate the effect of daylighting (from windows or skylights) on student academic performance in elementary school classrooms across three different school districts.

participants.description: Over 21,000 second through fifth grade students from three elementary school districts in Orange County, California (Capistrano), Seattle, Washington, and Fort Collins, Colorado.
participants.recruitment: Student performance data obtained from three elementary school districts.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Daylighting conditions in over 2000 classrooms were classified using a 0-5 scale for window size/tint, presence/type of skylighting, and overall expected daylight. Specific categories included 'Daylight, Min. to Max.', 'Windows, Min. to Max.', 'Skylight A' (well-designed, diffused, controllable), 'Skylight B' (poorly designed, clear acrylic, no controls, direct glare), 'Operable Windows', and 'Skylight Monitor' (Fort Collins).

measures.instrument: Capistrano Core Level Tests (RIT points) for math and reading, administered Fall 1997 and Spring 1998.
Iowa Test of Basic Skills (ITBS), Form M (NCE Scale 1-99) for math and reading, administered Spring 1998 (Seattle).
Northwest Educational Association 'level' tests (normalized RIT points) for math and reading, administered Spring 1998 (Fort Collins).

mechanisms: Improved Visibility Due to Higher Illumination Levels: Daylit classrooms have 2-3 times higher illumination levels, increasing task visibility, speed, and accuracy.

Improved Visibility Due to Improved Light Quality: Daylight provides better light distribution (more even, stronger vertical component), better color rendition (continuous spectrum), absence of flicker (compared to magnetic ballast fluorescents), and sparkle/highlights on 3D objects (semi-directional lighting, making objects more memorable and setting livelier).

Improved Health: Exposure to daylight increases Vitamin D, treats Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), regulates circadian rhythms, suppresses melatonin (increasing alertness), and may influence immunological functions and reduce risks of estrogen-related cancers.
Daylight Deprivation: Children in climates with less overall sun exposure (Seattle, Fort Collins) may be more sensitive to classroom daylight exposure, leading to larger positive effects.

Improved Mood: Daylight is perceived as 'natural' and 'makes people feel better' or happier, directly improving student mood and indirectly improving teacher mood, which in turn positively affects students' calm and attention spans.

Higher Arousal Levels: High illumination levels suppress melatonin, keeping children more alert and capable of absorbing new information. Variability of daylight may also contribute to higher arousal and interest throughout the day.

Improved Behavior: Strong correlations between daylight and student behavior, particularly sociability and concentration. Daylit environments may support typical seasonal and daily hormone rhythms, influencing concentration, cooperation, body growth, and sick leave.
moderators: Skylight design (diffusing lens, controls, direct sunlight)
Participation in Gifted and Talented (GATE) programs
Air conditioning presence (Capistrano, with preliminary negative association)
Teacher operation of shades (Fort Collins skylights)
implementation_implications: Daylighting systems should block direct sunlight penetration into classrooms.
Daylighting systems should allow teachers to control the amount of daylight entering the classroom.
Well-designed skylights (diffused, controllable) are beneficial, while poorly designed ones (clear acrylic, no controls, direct glare) can be detrimental.
Operable windows are a positive feature, regardless of air conditioning, suggesting benefits from natural ventilation.

limitations: The statistical study cannot prove causation, only association between variables.
Less detailed analysis for Seattle and Fort Collins districts, increasing the probability of unaccounted confounding factors.
Greatest likelihood of unknown variables influencing findings in Fort Collins due to limited information on student/school characteristics.
Limited range of window conditions in Fort Collins may have led to unreported effects for maximum window area.
Weak skylighting effect in Fort Collins likely due to poor lighting quality from south-facing monitors and teachers keeping shades closed.
Lack of year-round observations of daylight illumination conditions in classrooms.
Study may be limited by not accounting for daylight exposure outside of the classroom.
Information about different types of electrical lighting used in schools was not available for Capistrano.
Information about air conditioning and natural ventilation was not included for Fort Collins.
Information about electric lighting was not included for Fort Collins.
